title: Gunnison County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Gunnison County well depths have a 70 ft median and 90th percentile of 350 ft. Learn what that means for yield, cost, and buying land on a well.
h1: Water wells in Gunnison County, Colorado
intro_html:
Gunnison County wells are classic high-country mountain wells: a lot of shallow producers in valley alluvium, and some very deep holes in fractured bedrock. The records cover 8,832 permits across the county, with 5,407 reporting a total depth and 1,992 listing a pump test yield. That’s enough data to get a realistic picture of what you’re signing up for on a rural property here.

I’ll walk through how deep wells actually run, how much water they make, what drilling costs look like in this terrain, and the main risks to check before you close on land or start building.

sections.heading: How deep Gunnison County wells really are
sections.html:
Across Gunnison County, the median well depth is 70 feet, and the middle half fall between 37 and 180 feet. So on a typical domestic well, you’re usually not chasing water thousands of feet down. That said, the 90th percentile sits at 350 feet, and the single deepest well on record goes down 4,207 feet, which shows how unpredictable fractured mountain bedrock can be when you’re in the wrong spot.

About 59% of wells are under 100 feet, another 27% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 12% land in the 300–600 foot range. Only 2% go deeper than 600. A driller bidding in this county will generally plan for something in that 37–180 foot middle band, but you should budget with the 350-foot tail in mind if you’re on higher or rocky ground.

sections.heading: Well yields and how much water to expect
sections.html:
Yield numbers in Gunnison County are solid for household use. The median reported pump test is 15 gpm, with the middle half between 7 and 15 gpm. For a typical exempt domestic well, that is more than enough for normal household demand, even with irrigation of a small lawn or garden within your permit terms.

Only 1% of tested wells report under 1 gpm, which is the “problem” category that often needs storage or careful management. About 12% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, 31% are in the 5–15 gpm bracket, and 57% exceed 15 gpm. Those numbers tell you that low-yield wells exist, but they’re the minority. If you’re evaluating a specific parcel, the smart move is to look up neighboring wells on the map and compare reported yields and depths around your site.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend in Gunnison County
sections.html:
Only 527 wells report a static water level, but the data we do have is encouraging. The overall median depth to water is 27 feet, with the middle half between 9 and 60 feet below surface. That’s fairly shallow for a mountain county and means pumps are not working excessively hard in most locations.

Looking by decade, median static levels have bounced around rather than showing a steady drop: about 45 feet in the 1970s, 18 in the 1980s, 22 in the 1990s, 16 in the 2000s, 30 in the 2010s, and 27 in the 2020s. That pattern looks like natural variability and development patterns more than a clear declining water table. Still, on higher benches or hard rock areas, your local conditions can differ, so treat this as county-wide background, not a guarantee for one lot.

sections.heading: Who’s been drilling and how activity has changed
sections.html:
Well development in Gunnison County picked up in the 1970s and really surged through the 1990s. The Division of Water Resources shows 43 permits from the 1950s and 80 in the 1960s, then a jump to 926 in the 1970s and 1,185 in the 1980s. The 1990s peak at 2,100 permits, followed by 1,501 in the 2000s, 837 in the 2010s, and 544 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit year on record is 2025, so drilling is very much ongoing.

Bob Williams Drilling Co. (Williams, Robert F.) dominates the records with 3,340 wells, with Shelton Drilling Corporation and Authorized (Pe, Pg) each logged on 253 wells. Most permits are for domestic or household use (about 76%), with smaller shares for stock, irrigation, and monitoring. You’ll also see most wells assigned to unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a handful in alluvial and Mancos units.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
Gunnison County sits on fractured mountain bedrock like granite and gneiss, which is slower, harder drilling than plains alluvium. Typical rig rates here run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county median depth of 70 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $4,600–$7,000.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete, ready-to-use well at that median depth often comes out around $10,600–$19,000. If your site or neighbors are in that 180–350 foot band, scale those numbers up accordingly. Before you buy, compare your lot’s elevation and geology with nearby completed wells so you’re not budgeting off the shallowest examples in the valley.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and building layout
sections.html:
Only a small share of wells report under 1 gpm, but with fractured bedrock there is always some risk of a low-yield or even dry hole on the wrong fracture pattern. That’s why reading yield and depth on adjacent parcels is critical. Most wells here target unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with just a few in Alluvial or Mancos, so performance can vary over short distances.

Within about 10 miles, there are 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 360 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those don’t mean your water is bad, but they’re a reason to test for metals and PFAS, not just bacteria. Plan your septic so it’s properly separated in elevation and distance from the well, and make sure your driveway, home site, and tank locations all work together before you start digging.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Gunnison County lot
sections.html:
When you’re evaluating a lot in Gunnison County, start by pulling the neighboring wells: look at their depths, yields, and static water levels. County-wide, a 70-foot median depth with 37–180 feet as the middle half means many wells are relatively shallow, but the 350-foot 90th percentile tells you not to ignore the deeper cases in your budgeting.

Most permits are domestic or household, so expect typical exempt-well rules and limits unless you’re in a special augmentation area. With a median yield of 15 gpm and a 27-foot median static water level, many properties have strong supply, but you still want a good pump test and water-quality lab work on any existing well. If no well is in yet, build your purchase contract or construction budget around the higher end of expected drilling depth in your immediate area, not the county median alone.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Gunnison County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Gunnison County, the median well depth is 70 feet, and the middle half of wells run between 37 and 180 feet. About 59% of wells are under 100 feet deep, another 27% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 12% are 300–600 feet. A small 2% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest recorded at 4,207 feet. Local geology and elevation drive where your well will fall in that range.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Gunnison County?
faq.a: Reported pump test data for 1,992 Gunnison County wells shows a median yield of 15 gpm, with the middle half between 7 and 15 gpm. Only about 1% of tested wells come in under 1 gpm, while 12% are 1–5 gpm, 31% fall in the 5–15 gpm range, and 57% exceed 15 gpm. For most homes, that’s plenty of capacity, but you should still review nearby wells for your specific parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Gunnison County, CO?
faq.a: In Gunnison County’s fractured bedrock, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county median depth of 70 feet, the borehole alone pencils out around $4,600–$7,000. Once you add casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete well at that depth commonly totals about $10,600–$19,000. If your area has many wells in the 180–350 foot range, plan your budget higher.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Gunnison County?
faq.a: The county has many domestic wells in use, but safety comes down to testing your specific well. Within roughly 10 miles there are 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, about 360 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those are reasons to lab-test for metals, PFAS, and bacteria. A good test panel and proper well construction are the right way to confirm potable water quality on a property here.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Gunnison County?
faq.a: Available static water level data from 527 wells does not show a simple long-term decline. Median depth to water by decade was about 45 feet in the 1970s, 18 in the 1980s, 22 in the 1990s, 16 in the 2000s, 30 in the 2010s, and 27 in the 2020s. Overall, the median static level is about 27 feet, with the middle half of readings between 9 and 60 feet. Conditions can still vary locally, so check nearby wells.
